1.pericope_label: Furthermore David the king said unto all the congregation, Solomon my son, whom alone God hath chosen, is yet young and tender, and the work is great: for the palace is not for man, but for the Lord God. Now I have prepared with all my might for the house of my God the gold for things to be made of gold, and the silver for things of silver, and the brass for things of brass, the iron for things of iron, and wood for things of wood; onyx stones, and stones to be set, glistering stones, and of divers colours, and all manner of precious stones, and marble stones in abundance. Moreover, because I have set my affection to the house of my God, I have of mine own proper good, of gold and silver, which I have given to the house of my God, over and above all that I have prepared for the holy house, Even three thousand talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and seven thousand talents of refined silver, to overlay the walls of the houses withal: The gold for things of gold, and the silver for things of silver, and for all manner of work to be made by the hands of artificers. And who then is willing to consecrate his service this day unto the Lord?

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses alone as of all his brothers and makes much of the word rendered palace: birah belongs to the later books and elsewhere always means the fortress-palace at Susa, this being the single place in Scripture where it is used of the Temple, well fitted by its associations to convey the magnificence the chronicler imagined. He then works through the materials word by word, noting that the Hebrew says only the gold for the gold, that the term rendered onyx is so uncertain the Greek translators gave it five different ways, that the stones to be set are strictly stones of fillings, that the glistering and party-coloured stones are stones of puk and riqmah, puk being the pigment used to darken brow and lash and so denoting colour, and that shayish is read nowhere else and means white marble. He puts the gold at eighteen million sterling and the silver at two million eight hundred thousand, places Ophir at Abhira near the mouth of the Indus, renders the verb for overlaying as strictly to besmear, and records the Syriac and Arabic reading of a thousand thousand talents. Keil and Delitzsch give thirteen and a half million pounds for the gold, or six and three quarters on the royal standard, take Ophir gold as the finest and best answering to the refined silver, and confine the overlaying to gold and silver leaf on the inner walls of the holy place, the most holy, the porch and the upper chambers.
Gill passes on two reckonings of the royal gift, thirty-six million six hundred and sixty thousand gold ducats after Scheuchzer, or thirteen and a half million pounds after Brerewood.

Clarke quotes the Targum that the palace was prepared not for the name of a son of man but for the name of the Word of the Lord God, prefers Parian for the marble since Paros among the Cyclade islands yielded the whitest and finest stone of antiquity and Josephus describes the temple as built of large polished blocks of it, and renders the closing appeal literally as filling the hand. Wesley says Ophir gold is the best and purest, divides the metals so that the temple walls took gold and the adjoining rooms silver beaten into plates, and reads the summons devotionally, that whoever engages in this service will find his hands full.

Henry reads the speech as a model of drawing others into a good work: no tax is laid, because what is done in piety should be done willingly and God loves a cheerful giver, and three reasons are offered instead, the youth of the successor, the greatness of a building meant not for man but for the Lord, and the example already set. He glosses with all my might as making it his business and takes it for a rule that work for God done with less brings nothing to pass.

debates.question: What were the three thousand talents of gold worth?

positions.position: About thirteen and a half million pounds, or six and three quarters reckoning by the royal shekel
Thirty-six million six hundred and sixty thousand ducats after Scheuchzer, or thirteen and a half million pounds after Brerewood

6.pericope_label: Then the chief of the fathers and princes of the tribes of Israel, and the captains of thousands and of hundreds, with the rulers of the king’s work, offered willingly, And gave for the service of the house of God of gold five thousand talents and ten thousand drams, and of silver ten thousand talents, and of brass eighteen thousand talents, and one hundred thousand talents of iron. And they with whom precious stones were found gave them to the treasure of the house of the Lord, by the hand of Jehiel the Gershonite. Then the people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly, because with perfect heart they offered willingly to the Lord: and David the king also rejoiced with great joy.

schools.summary: Ellicott points out that chief, princes, captains and rulers all render a single Hebrew word, so the verse names one class described four ways with the stewards of the royal domains added, and he takes the particle before them as inclusive. He puts the five thousand talents of gold at between thirty and forty millions sterling, the silver at about four million with Schrader's lower estimate of three and three quarters noted, and remarks that bronze and iron were worth far more then than now. On the darics he names Darius son of Hystaspes as the first to strike them, observes that they stayed current in Western Asia long after Persia fell and that the Hebrew word recurs only at Ezra, and draws the conclusion that since no real coins appear in Scripture before the exile the chronicler or his source substituted a familiar currency for an older expression of value. Keil and Delitzsch identify the stewards with the officials catalogued earlier, deny that the Hebrew answers to the Greek drachma or the Arabic dirhem, derive it from the daric on the evidence of the Syriac rendering, value the coin at about twenty-two shillings and sixpence, and cite the numismatic literature for surviving specimens.

Gill calls the first group the princes of the twelve tribes, and on the rejoicing observes that the people were glad not only to have something to offer but to find themselves and others quite free to do it.

Clarke works from a talent of five thousand and seventy-five pounds odd and reaches over twenty-five million sterling for the gold, noting that Dr Prideaux's higher estimate would raise it considerably, computes the silver at something over three and a half million, values the daric at about twenty shillings, and alone converts the base metals, turning the brass into something past a thousand tons and the iron into some five thousand seven hundred. Wesley finds three things in the general gladness, the grace of God working in the givers, a token of divine favour toward them, and a pledge that the long-desired building would now go up quickly, and adds that it is a great reviving for good men leaving the world to see those they leave behind zealous for it.

Henry insists that although the people were persuaded into giving they gave willingly and with a perfect heart, which is said by one who knew their hearts, and that they gave like princes of Israel. He reads the rejoicing two ways, either the givers pleased at the chance to honour God and at the prospect of the work finished, or the commons pleased with rulers so forward in it, and traces the king's own joy to seeing the fruit of his psalms and other helps to devotion and to knowing his successor would be surrounded by such men.

debates.question: What were the five thousand talents of gold and ten thousand talents of silver worth?

positions.position: Between thirty and forty millions sterling for the gold, about four million for the silver, or three and three quarters on Schrader Assyrian data
Over twenty-five million for the gold, more on Prideaux higher estimate of the talent, and something over three and a half million for the silver
Twenty-two and a half millions for the gold, or eleven and a half on the royal standard

outliers.claim: Argues that because no real coins are named anywhere in Scripture before the exile, the chronicler or his authority must have substituted the daric, a currency familiar to his own readers, for whatever expression of value the older record used

10.pericope_label: Wherefore David blessed the Lord before all the congregation: and David said, Blessed be thou, Lord God of Israel our father, for ever and ever. Thine, O Lord, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty: for all that is in the heaven and in the earth is thine; thine is the kingdom, O Lord, and thou art exalted as head above all. Both riches and honour come of thee, and thou reignest over all; and in thine hand is power and might; and in thine hand it is to make great, and to give strength unto all. Now therefore, our God, we thank thee, and praise thy glorious name.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch frame the prayer by its occasion, the decree having given the building to the peace-king rather than the man of war, so that the old servant of the Lord prepared what he could and now found the chiefs willing, seeing in that willingness a particular proof of divine favour with which he closes the last parliament of his reign. Ellicott sets the piece in literary history: the spirit that once found its outlet in the odes of psalmists and the trumpet-tones of prophets ran, when psalmody had weakened and prophecy died, into impassioned prayer, and he is careful to say the chronicler or his source puts the utterance into the aged king's mouth. He insists the opening words join as Israel our father rather than Jehovah our father, adding that the divine fatherhood never became a governing idea within Old Testament limits, renders the doxology from eternity even unto eternity, unpicks the vocabulary of the great ascription, and suspects a pronoun has dropped out twice. On the closing thanks both note the participles, which make it a praise continually rising afresh.

Gill ascribes to God the ability and the willingness alike, knowing who works in men both to will and to do, and on the twelfth verse observes that whatever men have of wealth or standing comes not from merit, diligence or good management but from providence, remarking that even the heathen made their gods the givers of riches.

Clarke contributes the Targum, which turns the ascription into a recital of history: the world created by that power, the fathers led out of Egypt, the passage of the Red Sea, the appearing on Sinai with troops of angels, the victories over Amalek and over Sihon and Og, the sun halted at Gibeon and the moon in Ajalon, and a kingdom in the firmament exalted over angels and over all earthly rulers. Wesley draws the lesson from the king's age, that it becomes the old and dying to have their hearts enlarged in praise, and that the nearer one comes to the world of everlasting praise the more its language should be spoken now.

Henry expects the prayer from what precedes, since a man who rejoices as this one did will make his rejoicing the matter of his thanksgiving, and notes that the blessing was public rather than private. On the great ascription he hears the stress fall on the definite article: not that God is great and powerful and glorious, but that his is the greatness, the power and the glory, which he holds in and of himself while every creature holds them derivatively.

outliers.claim: Reads the prayer as evidence of a shift in the channel of inspiration, the spirit that once produced psalmody and prophecy finding its outlet in later days in impassioned prayer instead

14.pericope_label: But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee. For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers: our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is none abiding. O Lord our God, all this store that we have prepared to build thee an house for thine holy name cometh of thine hand, and is all thine own. I know also, my God, that thou triest the heart, and hast pleasure in uprightness. As for me, in the uprightness of mine heart I have willingly offered all these things: and now have I seen with joy thy people, which are present here, to offer willingly unto thee. O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, our fathers, keep this for ever in the imagination of the thoughts of the heart of thy people, and prepare their heart unto thee: And give unto Solomon my son a perfect heart, to keep thy commandments, thy testimonies, and thy statutes, and to do all these things, and to build the palace, for the which I have made provision.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the idiom of the fourteenth verse as holding strength together, a phrase confined to Chronicles and Daniel, and explain the strangers and sojourners by tenure, the land being held in usufruct only and everything else a man has along with it, a loan committed rather than a possession. Ellicott counts the same nine occurrences of the phrase, presses the closing word of the fifteenth verse to mean no hope and no assured future, and asks what the plaintive turn is for, answering that it emphasises what precedes, since creatures of a day can hold nothing absolutely. Both take the appeal to the searcher of hearts as warrant for the claim to have given without grudging, Ellicott spelling out that the motive was glory and not self-interest, and both render the petition for the people as asking that the present frame of mind be given permanence and the heart directed rather than merely prepared.

Gill puts the self-abasement as dust and ashes receiving an honour it has no claim to, and pauses over the scale of the store to report two computations, Jacob Leon reckoning the gold at tens of thousands of tons and the silver at nearly as much, Witsius bringing both together at something over twenty thousand tons of gold, doubled again if these were sanctuary talents.

Clarke glosses sojourners as lodging for a night in another man's house, finds in the closing clause not merely impermanence but the absence of any expectation of exemption from the changes the fathers met, and adds the Targum, which makes the days a bird's shadow flying through the air of heaven with no hope to any man of living for ever; on the prayer he says the dispositions came from God and must be sustained by the same means. Wesley reads the wonder as double, that God should give both the wealth to offer and the willing mind to offer it, speaks of the land in the language of estate, tenants and not proprietors, draws the inference that men give God only what they must shortly leave and cannot keep so that his accepting it is itself a favour, extends the acknowledgement beyond money to every good thought, desire and work, and prefers confirm to prepare on the ground that what grace began grace must carry on.

Henry notices how odd the humility looks in context, the speaker being at the height of his standing, presiding over a great assembly, naming his heir and making a magnificent gift, and in that posture calling himself and the most honourable nation then alive unworthy of notice. He turns the brevity of life into an argument against merit, since a service confined to so narrow a span can pretend to earn nothing, and observes that the speaker puts himself at the front of those who must own their days a shadow though his own life had as much substance in it as most; he attaches the caution he thinks the princes needed, that none should reckon they had merited anything, what they returned being a small part of what they had received.

outliers.claim: Reports two seventeenth-century computations of the accumulated temple treasure, Jacob Leon reckoning the gold at tens of thousands of tons and Witsius bringing gold and silver together at something over twenty thousand tons, doubled again if the talents were those of the sanctuary

20.pericope_label: And David said to all the congregation, Now bless the Lord your God. And all the congregation blessed the Lord God of their fathers, and bowed down their heads, and worshipped the Lord, and the king. And they sacrificed sacrifices unto the Lord, and offered burnt offerings unto the Lord, on the morrow after that day, even a thousand bullocks, a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel: And did eat and drink before the Lord on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and anointed him unto the Lord to be the chief governor, and Zadok to be priest.

schools.summary: Ellicott removes a false note of time, the now of the summons being a particle of entreaty rather than a temporal adverb, suspects the response used a set liturgical form like the doxologies closing the books of the Psalter, and traces the two gestures precisely, a bowing which the Greek renders sometimes as bending the knee and usually as stooping, and a full prostration, noting that the pair is almost never separated. He observes that the phrase for the morrow occurs here only, grounds the homage paid to the king in his standing as representative, and calls the anointing of Zadok a notice remarkable and peculiar to this book which illustrates the almost sovereign dignity of the high priesthood and shows that the removal of Abiathar was already contemplated. Keil and Delitzsch note the same fixed collocation of the gestures, set out the sacrifice as a thousand bullocks, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs for burnt offering with matching libations and thank offerings in quantity so that all present could share the meal, take the phrase to Jehovah as meaning in accordance with his will since the preposition will not bear the sense of before, and infer that Zadok received the high priesthood with the consent of the estates of the kingdom.
Gill identifies the congregation as princes, captains and officers, and places the eating and drinking before the ark, in the tent that had been pitched for it.

Clarke distinguishes the reverence given to God as supreme Ruler from that given to the king as his deputy, reports the Targum putting the libations at a thousand so as to equal the victims, describes the second class of sacrifice as peace offerings whose flesh the people ate, recalls the first anointing as done in haste and without pomp while Adonijah reached for the throne, holds this second ceremony to have taken place with full rites once everything was quiet and the father probably dead, and states the principle that God never surrendered his own right to be king in Israel. Wesley calls the one worship religious and the other civil, agrees about the emergency of the first anointing, and denies that this ceremony made Zadok high priest at all, since a high priest might have a deputy and the act settled only the reversion after Abiathar death, which is why Abiathar went on exercising the office until he was thrust out.

Henry cautions that whoever speaks for a congregation, only those share the benefit who join him, and that joining is done less by bowing the head than by lifting the soul; he takes the throne Solomon sat on as the throne of the Lord and reads his kingdom as a type of the kingdom of the Messiah, whose throne is that same throne.

debates.question: What did the anointing of Zadok effect?

positions.position: It conferred the high priesthood, with the consent of the estates of the kingdom
It illustrates the almost sovereign dignity of the office and shows that the deposition of Abiathar was already in David mind
It made him nothing yet, settling only the reversion after Abiathar death, since Abiathar continued in office until Solomon thrust him out

outliers.claim: Holds that the second anointing took place after David was probably already dead, the first having been hurried through without pomp during the attempt of Adonijah

23.pericope_label: Then Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord as king instead of David his father, and prospered; and all Israel obeyed him. And all the princes, and the mighty men, and all the sons likewise of king David, submitted themselves unto Solomon the king. And the Lord magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and bestowed upon him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott warns against reading an abdication into the phrase about reigning instead of his father, since the paragraph anticipates the reign that follows and stands here as the immediate sequel of the coronation; he distinguishes the princes, who are the officers listed earlier, from the king's sons, notes that the construction rendered submitted themselves occurs nowhere else and looks different from the familiar giving of the hand in token of good faith, so that some ancient mode of homage may be meant, records the Latin expansion into two acts, and counts only two predecessors on the throne, or three if Ishbosheth is included. Keil and Delitzsch hold that a history of David reign would be incomplete without these verses, since they record the fulfilment of what he had asked for his son, reject outright the derivation of the idiom from any custom of clasping hands in swearing, and reach the same count by grammar, the construction meaning simply none and implying no more than that there had been more than one king before.

Gill reads the throne of the Lord as vicegerency, the occupant ruling a people that are not his own over a throne given and established for him, and takes the magnifying to lie in the large share of wisdom and understanding given for governing.

Clarke translates the idiom literally, they gave the hand under Solomon, and identifies it with the oath-taking ceremony of putting the hand beneath the thigh. Wesley explains the title of the throne by the peculiar kingship of God over Israel, who had both the founding and the filling of it by immediate direction.

Henry gives the fullest account of the throne of the Lord, which is not the throne prepared in the heavens but the throne of Israel, so named because God founded and filled it by direct appointment, their civil laws being divine and Urim and prophets serving their princes as a privy council. He accepts the derivation of the gesture from the oath ceremony but offers an alternative beside it, that the phrase may express devotion so entire that a man would put his hand under another feet to serve him; he observes that the brothers whose seniority gave them the prior title submitted anyway, because God both made this son king and made him fit to be one, and sets the contrast with the father, a better man who came to the crown with much difficulty and by slow steps, having more faith and so having it more tried. Of the greatness conferred he thinks the man's very countenance and presence must have had something awful in them.

debates.question: What does the idiom rendered submitted themselves describe?

positions.position: The oath-taking ceremony of putting the hand beneath the thigh
Possibly instead a devotion so entire as to put the hand under another feet in service
Some ancient mode of doing homage, the construction being unparalleled and distinct from giving the hand in token of good faith
Not derived from any custom of clasping hands in swearing

outliers.claim: Insists that the phrase about reigning instead of his father implies no abdication, the whole paragraph being anticipative of Solomon reign rather than a record of David stepping down

themes: Then Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord as king instead of David his father, and prospered; and all Israel obeyed him.

26.pericope_label: Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel. And the time that he reigned over Israel was forty years; seven years reigned he in Hebron, and thirty and three years reigned he in Jerusalem. And he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour: and Solomon his son reigned in his stead. Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer, With all his reign and his might, and the times that went over him, and over Israel, and over all the kingdoms of the countries.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers the pluperfect, David had reigned, reads the phrase over all Israel as pointing back to the period when only Judah acknowledged him, notes that the verse on the length of the reign duplicates the notice in Kings with two words dropped and that the seven years at Hebron were more exactly seven and a half, prefers the literal satisfied with days for the obituary formula and quotes the Syriac, and stays with the Hebrew term for acts, which means a matter or transaction as readily as a word, so that Gesenius could render the phrase as a book entitled The Acts of Samuel. Keil and Delitzsch make the same correction to the years at Hebron, read the same allusion in over all Israel, refer the question of the cited authorities to the introduction, and gloss the times that went over him as the seasons of joy and sorrow, identifying the kingdoms of the countries as Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon and Aram.

Gill calls the reign long and glorious, gives the age at death as seventy, and takes the acts first and last to cover what was memorable before the accession as well as the reigns at Hebron and Jerusalem.

Clarke breaks the obituary formula into four and dwells on each, an age long enough that living further could not be desired, days full in the sense of seeing everything accomplished or well forward, riches attested by the sums left for the temple, and honour beyond any crowned head before or since; he holds the sources all lost except what survives scattered in the later books, and insists that none of the books we now possess are the records here cited. He closes with Delaney's character of David, a peasant by birth and a prince by merit, hero in youth, monarch in manhood and saint in age, calling the matter of Uriah the great and only blot. Wesley explains the seam, the writer having described the settlement of the heir and now returning to his main business, makes satisfied the point of the obituary since the man had enough of this world and knew when he had enough, and locates the sources in the chronicles of the kingdom kept by Nathan and Gad as historiographers, out of which later hands selected under divine direction what would serve the church.

Henry observes that forty years was the term of Moses, of several judges, of Saul before him and of Solomon after, and says the obituary both ways, that the king was loaded with days, riches and honour and also satiated with them, noting that a soldier from his youth was preserved through every danger and died in his bed yet in the bed of honour, and adding that a good man will soon be full of such things but never satisfied with them. He has the registers begun by Samuel in his lifetime and continued after his death by Nathan and Gad, says flatly that they were then in being but are now lost, and draws the lesson that good use may be made of church histories authentic without being inspired.

debates.question: What were the books of Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and do they survive?

positions.position: Registers begun by Samuel and continued by Nathan and Gad, then in being but now lost
Lost except for what survives scattered in the later books, and certainly not the canonical books we now possess
The chronicles of the kingdom kept by Nathan and Gad as historiographers, from which later hands selected under divine direction
A question of the chronicler cited authorities, referred to the introduction

outliers.claim: Closes the chapter with Delaney extended character of David, from peasant by birth and prince by merit to hero in youth, monarch in manhood and saint in age, treating the matter of Uriah as the single blot on it
